claim: Phase v26 trained a Liquid Neural Net (LNN) — adapted from the enzyme_Software/liquid_nn_v2 architecture (ContextAwareTauPredictor + EdgeAwareMessagePassing + adaptive-tau ODE-style 4-step integration over operon-graph edges) — on the same 6-organism multi-bacterial dataset as v25 (Caulobacter, S. aureus, M. tb, S. Typhimurium, A. baylyi, M. pneumoniae; 13,496 genes total with paired Tn-seq / TraDIS / deletion-mutant essentiality calls), tested on Syn3A held out (455 genes, Breuer 2019). Two LNN variants tried: (1) full LNN with structured scalar features (20) + 3-mer codon counts (64) + 4-mer counts (256) + operon-edge graph passing, hidden=128, 4 ODE steps, 80 epochs (~133k parameters); (2) smaller LNN without k-mers, hidden=64, 3 ODE steps, dropout=0.2, weight_decay=1e-3, 60 epochs (~29k parameters). Result: BOTH LNN variants UNDERPERFORM the gradient-boosting baseline on the cross-organism Syn3A test. Variant 1 test MCC = 0.0391 (honest threshold from training); the model collapsed by predicting 99.3% essential because the train→test class-balance flip (16% → 84% essential) shifted the calibration. Variant 2 test MCC = 0.1234 (honest), 0.1955 (with optimal-on-test threshold — diagnostic ceiling, not honest). Both are below v25's GB at 0.2268 and below v24's mpne→syn3a annotation-only at 0.2034. The LNN's pooled-training MCC was 0.46-0.52 (reasonable within-organism), but the per-gene probability distribution on Syn3A compressed into [0.85, 1.00] for 95%+ of genes — indicating loss of discriminative power under the cross-organism distribution shift. Trees (gradient boosting) carve out specific feature regions and threshold-tune naturally; smooth-boundary neural networks learn organism-specific calibrations that don't transfer when the test organism's class prior is dramatically different.
source_detail: Reproducible via scripts/train_lnn_essentiality.py (full LNN with k-mers, 80 epochs); the smaller-LNN variant was an in-line probe in the training session. Inputs: outputs/multiorg_per_gene_features.csv (built by scripts/build_multiorg_features.py from 6 essentiality supps + 6 GenBanks committed at commits 0fe6b88 and e615fd6). Output: outputs/lnn_essentiality_results.json. Test set: Syn3A 455-gene Breuer 2019 panel.
caveats: Class-balance distribution shift dominates. Training organisms aggregate to 16% essential (5-15% per organism for non-Mycoplasma); Syn3A test is 84% essential. Neural networks learn smooth decision boundaries calibrated to the training class prior; when applied to a test set with a flipped prior, predictions cluster in the high-confidence range (98% > 0.9 for v1, 71% > 0.9 for v2) and threshold tuning on training selects a threshold that's wrong for the test distribution. Trees (gradient boosting) handle this naturally because tree splits are local to specific feature regions and threshold tuning operates per-leaf rather than globally.

The LNN's adaptive-tau and operon-edge graph passing did NOT add value on this task. Operon edges connect ~20-30% of genes within each organism, but the graph patterns differ between organisms (operon structure varies by lineage), so message passing introduces organism-specific signal rather than organism-invariant essentiality signal. The k-mer features were the worst offender — codon bias varies by GC content (Mycoplasma ~30% GC vs E. coli ~50% GC), so k-mer counts ARE organism-identifying rather than function-identifying.

Removing k-mers (variant 2) tripled the honest cross-organism MCC (0.04 → 0.12) and halved the parameter count (133k → 29k). This tells us the LNN's capacity exceeded what the available training data supports for cross-organism transfer. Smaller models with fewer organism-specific features generalize better across the species barrier.

Diagnostic-ceiling MCC (threshold tuned on test, NOT honest hold-out): variant 1 = 0.0964, variant 2 = 0.1955. Even with cheating threshold calibration, neither LNN variant reaches GB's honest 0.2268. This rules out the explanation 'LNN learned but threshold was wrong' — the LNN's representational ceiling on this task is below GB's.

What WOULD help (untested): domain adversarial training (forcing the LNN to learn organism-invariant features), per-organism batch normalization (rescaling features per organism), CORAL-style domain alignment, much more training data (many more bacteria), or a different architecture entirely (e.g. attention-based transformer with relative-position embeddings instead of operon-graph LNN).

The honest read: for cross-organism essentiality prediction with the available 14k-gene multi-bacterial dataset, gradient boosting is the appropriate model. Neural-net architectural cleverness (LNN, transformers, GNN) needs much more data or domain-shift handling to beat tree-based baselines. v25's GB at 0.2268 stands as the best cross-organism Syn3A predictor on this dataset.

Confidence: measured (the LNN training is reproducible, both variants were trained to convergence, the cross-organism transfer failure is robustly demonstrated by the per-gene probability histograms, and the comparison to GB is apples-to-apples on the same training/test split). The verdict 'LNN underperforms GB' is the cleanest read; treating either LNN variant as having beaten GB would require optimal-on-test threshold tuning which is methodologically inadmissible.
